mcqs.question: What's the core mechanism for turning a growth forecast into an actionable capacity plan?
options: Wait until utilization hits 90% before starting any procurement conversation
Project forward from the growth rate to find the crossing date, add a buffer for lead time, and set a trigger that fires early enough to act before the crossing
Always double current capacity immediately regardless of growth rate
Ignore lead time since cloud capacity can always be added instantly
mcqs.explanation: The trigger threshold, set by working backward from lead time, is what makes a forecast operational rather than just informational. Waiting for a fixed utilization number ignores lead time, doubling capacity blindly ignores actual need, and not every component can be added instantly.

mcqs.question: A service crosses its 140K QPS ceiling in projected quarter 4, and new read replicas take 2 quarters to provision. When should procurement start?
options: At quarter 4, exactly when the ceiling is projected to be crossed
Only after the ceiling has actually been breached in production
Around quarter 2, since the 2-quarter lead time must be subtracted from the quarter-4 crossing date
Never — rely on the existing 40% headroom indefinitely
mcqs.explanation: Starting at the crossing date itself means the new capacity arrives 2 quarters late, since the lead time has to be subtracted from the projected crossing, not added after it. Waiting for an actual breach or relying on headroom forever both ignore that the ceiling is coming regardless.

mcqs.question: Growth isn't perfectly linear — how should an uncertain forecast be handled?
options: Plan against a range of conservative, expected, and aggressive growth curves, set the action trigger off the conservative one, and revisit regularly
Assume growth will always match last year's exact rate with no need for revision
Only plan for the most aggressive possible growth scenario, regardless of cost
Skip forecasting entirely and react only once metrics show a real problem
mcqs.explanation: Ranging the forecast and triggering off the conservative case avoids being caught out by growth that outpaces a single point estimate, while regular revisits keep the plan current. Assuming a fixed rate, over-planning for worst-case only, or abandoning forecasting all carry needless risk or cost.

mcqs.question: Why is waiting until 90% utilization to start a capacity conversation risky for a component with a multi-quarter procurement lead time?
options: Utilization above 90% always means the service is about to fail immediately
Procurement lead times don't apply to cloud-hosted infrastructure
Waiting is fine as long as the team is notified promptly once it happens
It guarantees hitting the capacity ceiling before the new capacity actually arrives, since the lead time hasn't been accounted for
mcqs.explanation: The math simply doesn't work: a multi-quarter lead time started at 90% utilization means the new capacity lands well after the ceiling is crossed. 90% isn't inherently catastrophic, lead times apply to plenty of cloud components too (managed tiers, quotas), and notification alone doesn't compress the lead time.
